Dr. Virendra Kumar
recalled that the
International Day of Older Persons
was observed across the country yesterday (October 1, 2026) and aids and assistive devices were distributed to
904 senior citizens at Bhavnagar, Gujarat on the occasion
. He appreciated the contribution of youth, NGOs and civil society organizations in facilitating such initiatives and supporting senior citizens.
Dr. Virendra Kumar observed that senior citizens often experience difficulties relating to
hearing, mobility and vision
with advancing age. He stated that the Ministry has decided to expand the distribution of assistive devices to beneficiaries residing in
Senior Citizens’ Homes across the country
, in consonance with the
Seva Sankalp Abhiyan
launched by the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on the completion of 25 years in governance.
The Minister emphasized that access to appropriate assistive devices can help senior citizens become
more self-reliant in carrying out their daily activities
and lead their lives with greater dignity and confidence.
Highlighting the significant contributions made by senior citizens in diverse fields, including
agriculture, literature and the armed forces
, Dr. Virendra Kumar noted that many elderly persons also face challenges arising from loneliness and social isolation. He emphasized the need for collective efforts to ensure that senior citizens are able to live their lives with
dignity, respect and honour
.
He called upon
youth, corporates, NGOs and organizations working for the welfare of senior citizens
to come forward and contribute towards building an inclusive society, in keeping with the vision of
Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas
outlined by the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi
.
Dr. Virendra Kumar further noted that, according to
Census 2011, India has 10.38 crore senior citizens
, with approximately
70 per cent residing in rural areas
. Emphasising the Government’s efforts to improve accessibility to welfare services, he stated that the Ministry plans to increase the number of
PM-Divya Asha Kendras from 109 to 300
so that senior citizens can access assistive devices and related services more conveniently and without undue waiting.
Addressing the gathering,
Shri B. L. Verma, Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment
, welcomed the senior citizens and highlighted the importance of the
Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana
, launched by the Department on
April 1, 2017
, under the guidance of the Hon’ble Prime Minister to benefit senior citizens in need of aids and assistive devices.
Shri B. L. Verma lauded the invaluable contributions and sacrifices made by senior citizens in the nation-building process. He also highlighted the initiatives being undertaken by the Department to promote
inter-generational bonding and reduce the generation gap
, while ensuring greater social inclusion and participation of senior citizens.
Shri Verma expressed the hope that senior citizens across the country would continue to contribute their experience, knowledge and wisdom towards realising the vision of
Viksit Bharat @2047
.
Shri Praveen Kumar, Chairman and Managing Director, ALIMCO, highlighted the performance and efficiency of ALIMCO in implementing the Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana under the guidance of Dr. Virendra Kumar. He also underscored the use of Artificial Intelligence by ALIMCO to better serve senior citizens in the coming years.
The programme concluded with the Hon’ble Ministers, along with the invited senior citizens, offering floral tributes to Mahatma Gandhi , Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri & Dr B R Ambedkar.
The programme reflects the Government’s continued commitment towards ensuring the dignity, independence and well-being of senior citizens, while strengthening access to aids and assistive devices and enabling them to lead a more self-reliant and dignified life.
The programme reflects the Government’s continued commitment to promoting the
dignity, independence, inclusion and well-being of senior citizens
. Through initiatives such as the Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana, the Government is strengthening access to assistive devices and enabling senior citizens, particularly those in need, to lead
more independent, self reliant, dignified and fulfilling lives
.
It is pertinent to mention that
Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana
(RVY)
is an initiative of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment aimed at providing physical aids and assisted-living devices to senior citizens in need, thereby supporting their mobility, independence and quality of life. The programme seeks to facilitate greater social inclusion and enable senior citizens to participate more independently in everyday life.

title: NITI Aayog organises National Workshop on SDG Budgeting in Kolkata under the State Support Mission, in collaboration with the Government of West Bengal and UNDP
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 OCT 2026 11:35AM by PIB Delhi
content:
NITI Aayog, in collaboration with the Government of West Bengal and with technical support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), organised a National Workshop on SDG Budgeting in Kolkata on 29 September 2026 under the State Support Mission (SSM) initiative of NITI Aayog. The Workshop focused on strengthening the alignment of planning and budgeting processes with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with emphasis on institutionalising SDG budget tagging and translating financial commitments into measurable development outcomes at the sub-national level.
The Workshop brought together participants from 32 States and Union Territories, along with senior officials from NITI Aayog, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) and its offices, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), Controller General of Accounts (CGA), Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), Indian Institute of Corporate Affairs (IICA), UNDP, UN Resident Coordinator Office (UNRCO), development partners, and representatives from FICCI, CII, SEBI, Tata Steel Foundation, Intellecap and GIZ. Government representatives from Haryana, Odisha, Meghalaya and West Bengal shared experiences on the implementation and institutionalisation of SDG Budgeting, reflecting the whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to SDG localisation.
The inaugural session was graced by Dr. Swapan Dasgupta, Hon'ble Finance Minister, Government of West Bengal; Dr. R. Balasubramaniam, Hon'ble Member, NITI Aayog; Shri K. Sanjay Murthy, Comptroller and Auditor General of India, virtually; Dr. V. Anantha Nageswaran, Chief Economic Adviser, Government of India, virtually; Shri Prabhat Kumar Mishra, Additional Chief Secretary, Finance, Government of West Bengal; Shri Stefan Priesner, United Nations Resident Coordinator; Dr. Angela Lusigi, Resident Representative, UNDP; and Shri Rajib Kumar Sen, Programme Director (SDGs), NITI Aayog.
Delivering the Chief Guest Address, Dr. Swapan Dasgupta said, "What we have not always had is a clean line running from a goal, to a target, to an allocation in the budget, to a unit that will actually spend. Without that line, the SDGs remain an aspiration on the asset side of the ledger with no corresponding entry on the liability side. SDG budget tagging is the discipline of drawing that line."
In his keynote address, Dr. R. Balasubramaniam said, "Mapping the SDGs to State expenditure is a significant step. Whole-of-society and whole-of-government can sound like slogans, but with the finance department, political leadership, multilateral institutions and the private sector together today, the idea becomes real. The task ahead is to guide every State so that money spent can be shown to be money spent wisely”.
Shri Prabhat Kumar Mishra, Additional Chief Secretary, Finance, Government of West Bengal, highlighted that the State has, for the first time, mapped its budget to the goal level of the SDGs and integrated the exercise into its Integrated Financial Management System.
Shri Stefan Priesner highlighted India’s enabling framework for private sector engagement, including CSR, Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting, ESG in capital markets and the Social Stock Exchange, and emphasised the need to integrate sustainability into core business decision-making. Dr. Angela Lusigi highlighted the value of SDG budget tagging in linking expenditure with specific SDG targets and assessing whether resources are reaching those who need them most, while also aligning CSR, investment and philanthropy with development priorities. She also noted the joint standards launched by ISO and UNDP to support public and private organisations in placing the SDGs at the core of decision-making.
The discussions emphasised that SDG budget tagging can enable governments to make expenditure visible against development goals, identify gaps and strengthen evidence-based planning. The “Guide on Mapping State Budgets to the SDGs”, developed jointly by NITI Aayog, the CAG of India and UNDP, was discussed as a practical framework for aligning State budgets with the Goals. The deliberations also underscored the importance of embedding SDG priorities within the annual budget cycle and establishing the institutional arrangements required to move from measurement to mission-mode implementation.
The workshop comprised four technical sessions covering the design elements of SDG budget tagging, including the identification of expenditure to be tagged, the appropriate level of tagging, linkage with the Head of Accounts, tagging to SDG Targets, attribution through NITI Aayog’s Scheme-SDG mapping and value assignment.
States including Haryana, Odisha, Meghalaya and West Bengal shared their experiences of implementation and institutionalisation. Discussions on integrating SDG budgeting into the annual budget cycle covered institutional responsibilities, reconciliation, quality assurance, reporting and performance audit.
The session on
“
Making It Happen: SDG Budgeting in the Annual Budget Cycle”, led by Shri Navneet Gupta, Principal Accountant General (A&E), examined the integration of SDG budget tagging into budget preparation, institutional responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms including reconciliation, quality assurance, reporting and performance audit, including the role of the CAG
A dedicated session on private sector engagement examined enabling policy frameworks, innovative financing and responsible business conduct to strengthen sustained private sector engagement with the SDGs. Representatives from Tata Steel Foundation, Intellecap, IICA, MoSPI, FICCI, GIZ, ITC Limited, CII and SEBI participated in the session.
As India advances towards Viksit Bharat@2047, with 2030 as a critical milestone for the SDGs, the workshop reaffirmed NITI Aayog’s commitment to strengthening cooperative federalism and supporting States and Union Territories in embedding the SDGs within their planning, budgeting and governance processes. The deliberations underscored the need to strengthen the linkage between public expenditure, development priorities and measurable outcomes, and to accelerate the transition from measurement to implementation.

title: Communicating Swachhata, Changing Behaviour
subtitle: The Social and Behaviour Change Communication Journey of the Swachh Bharat Mission
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 OCT 2026 1:58PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) placed behaviour change at the centre of sanitation
, moving beyond infrastructure towards sustained practices and social norms.
Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC)
transformed communication from information dissemination into dialogue, participation, and collective action.
Mahatma Gandhi
and his ideals of cleanliness and
self-service
became the guiding principles of SBM. Community institutions and grassroots actors, like
Swachhagrahis,
helped turn individual sanitation practices into shared community norms.
Multiple communication channels
reinforced Swachhata messages across households, communities, public spaces and digital platforms. Women and children became both beneficiaries and
active agents
in spreading and sustaining sanitation behaviours. Reinforcement, recognition, incentives and participatory monitoring helped move Swachhata from a campaign activity to sustained community behaviour.
The Behavioural Foundations of Swachh Bharat
The
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)
has treated sanitation as a matter of
behaviour
,
participation
and
collective responsibility
. The Mission recognised that infrastructure alone could not create sustained sanitation outcomes. SBM therefore placed
behaviour change communication
at the centre of its implementation approach. Under SBM-G, the focus is not limited to toilet construction. It encourages communities to adopt safe and sustainable sanitation practices. Similarly, under SBM-U, the focus is not only on waste processing. It focusses on making waste segregation at source a public habit and achieving total urban sanitation and public cleanliness.
Information, Education, Communication (
IEC) strategies
,
behaviour reinforcement,
and
monitoring
are therefore integral to the SBM implementation strategy. SBM has evolved from building sanitation assets towards sustaining sanitation behaviour. This evolution places
Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC)
at the centre.
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)
Launched on 2 October 2014, SBM became one of
India’s largest government-led sanitation movements
. The Mission operates through two components:
SBM-Grameen
and
SBM-Urban
. SBM-G focuses on rural sanitation, toilet access, usage, and waste management. SBM-U focuses on urban sanitation, waste management, and clean public spaces. For details on achievements of SBM, please also read
here.
From Information to Behaviour Change
Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC) uses communication to support positive social change.
It combines several approaches to influence knowledge, attitudes, norms and practices. These include
interpersonal communication
,
community mobilisation
and
mass media
. It also includes
social media
,
entertainment
,
advocacy
and
strategic partnerships
.
SBCC under SBM goes beyond simply disseminating information. It seeks to influence attitudes, social norms and everyday practices. This approach under SBM combines
interpersonal communication, community mobilisation, awareness generation and collective action
. Its long-term objective is to change social norms around open defecation and waste management. It recognises that people’s behaviour is influenced by their social environment. Families, neighbours, community groups, local institutions and trusted leaders can reinforce or discourage particular practices.
Communication, therefore, works through relationships and collective participation
.
Mahatma Gandhi: A Moral Anchor for SBCC under SBM
Mahatma Gandhi’s emphasis on cleanliness and sanitation provided a powerful foundation for the SBM’s communication strategy. The Mission was launched on 2 October 2014 to achieve a Swachh Bharat by Gandhi’s 150th birth anniversary in 2019. The logo of SBM represents the spectacles of Mahatma Gandhi. It has helped in creating the brand value and representing the emotion for cleanliness worldwide. It has also helped the masses associate themselves easily and quickly with the mission. Consequently, rural India was declared ODF on 2 October 2019.
Image
1
: The logo of SBM
Mahatma Gandhi had started his campaign for cleanliness from Champaran during the Satyagraha movement.
His vision of an ideal village was one with perfect sanitation, village lanes and streets free of all avoidable dust. In his book
“
Ashram Observances in Action
”,
Gandhi writes that
sanitary service is an essential and sacred service
. His
Sevagram Ashram
laid emphasis on engaging no outside labour for this work. The members themselves attended in turns to clean the premises. The Ashram rules also laid down that it was necessary that inmates wash their hands and wipe them with a clean napkin.
SBM’s messaging drew on this legacy
to build public ownership and encourage participation in behaviour change.
This connection also shaped the language and symbolism of the behaviour change movement. The term ‘
Swachhagrahi’
consciously drew from Gandhi’s tradition of
Satyagraha
, recasting citizens and sanitation volunteers as participants in a collective
Swachhagraha
. SBM, therefore, revered Mahatma Gandhi not merely as a commemorative figure, but as a
communication anchor
for linking cleanliness with collective action, citizenship and sustained behavioural change.
Taking Behaviour Change to the Doorsteps: Changing Individual Habits
SBM translated SBCC principles into direct, community-level engagement.
Interpersonal Communication (IPC)
became an important pathway for influencing sanitation practices. Unlike one-way messaging, IPC enables
dialogue
between communicators and community members
. It allows concerns, perceptions, and practical barriers to be discussed within
local contexts
. The government relied on frontline workers, Swachhagrahis, community leaders, self-help groups (SHGs), and existing social networks for
facilitating IPC
. The
methods
included home visits, face-to-face counselling, small-group sessions, peer communication and discussions at homes, health centres, community settings and religious gatherings.
Swachhagrahis
became grassroots foot soldiers and motivators under
SBM-G.
Their role extended beyond promoting toilet construction. They helped families adopt and sustain safe sanitation behaviours. Swachhagrahis facilitated
community nudging
and
triggering
, household visits, and sanitation discussions. They also supported community mobilisation and strengthened
Nigrani Samitis
. Their engagement continued even after ODF declaration to further reinforce sanitation practices among individuals and families.
Image 2: A meeting of Swachhagrahis and SHG
didis in Bihar
Image 3: Nigrani Samiti using interpersonal communication to spread the message of swachhata
Interpersonal communication also extended into
community-led vigilance
through
Nigrani Samitis
. These committees were strengthened to support ODF achievement and sustainability. Their activities included
regular morning and evening monitoring
within villages. Nigrani activities focused particularly on
common open defecation spots
. They reinforced sanitation messages through continued community presence and follow-up. Regular Nigrani drives, village meetings, and
Ratri Chaupals
helped sustain ODF behaviour. Swachhagrahis were provided with a
toolkit
that included a
torch and whistle
to support their field-level vigilance during community monitoring.
The approach therefore moved sanitation from an individual practice towards a shared community norm.
The community itself became an active participant in reinforcing and sustaining behaviour change.
From Individual Conversations to Collective Action
Interpersonal communication created opportunities for dialogue at the household and community level. Community mobilisation took this process further by bringing people together to discuss shared sanitation concerns and identify collective solutions. Under SBM, it provided platforms for communities to participate in decisions affecting their everyday sanitation practices.
Gram Sabhas, chaupals, community meetings
and other local forums enabled dialogue on sanitation issues and helped communities build consensus around common priorities.
Community mobilisation also brought different groups into the sanitation conversation.
Community leaders, Panchayati Raj Institutions, volunteers, religious leaders and women’s groups
could facilitate local discussions and events. This approach connected individual behaviour with collective responsibility. A household adopting safe sanitation practices became part of a wider community effort.
Community discussions
created opportunities to identify local concerns, exchange experiences, and build agreement around desired practices. This approach was also reflected through campaigns such as
Chalo Champaran, Swachh Shakti, Swachh Sundar Sauchalaya, Swachhata Hi Seva, Swachh Sundar Samudayik Sauchalaya, Swachh Bharat Diwas, Swachhata Mahotsav and Swachhata Pakhwada
. These campaigns provided platforms for collective participation around sanitation and cleanliness.
Image
4
: A wall painting in Assam spreading swachhata messages in local language
Community mobilisation was further reinforced through
mid-media and outdoor communication
. These channels carried sanitation messages beyond individual conversations and into spaces where communities routinely gathered.
Puppet shows, magic shows, drama
and
street theatre
(nukkad natak)
are some of the examples of local and traditional mid-media formats. Outdoor media uses public spaces such as
billboards and wall paintings
on
authorised public walls
to communicate sanitation messages. Wall paintings and
graffiti
art
have been used especially to communicate Swachhata messages while reflecting local identity and supporting city beautification. The importance of such formats lies not only in message visibility, but also in how they place Swachhata within the everyday social environment. A sanitation message encountered during a community event, street performance, or public gathering can reinforce conversations taking place within households and local groups.
A major area of focus under SBM-U has been the
leveraging of digital tools
for maximizing citizen outreach. For example,
Google Maps
was used to upload of more than
67,000 public toilet blocks
across more than
3,300 cities.
This has made sanitation facilities more easily accessible to all categories of citizens. The
Swachhata App
has provided a one-stop digital platform for grievance redressal for citizens to register their complaints about any aspect of cleanliness.
Image
5
: Swachhata App available for both Android and iOS users
Mass media
provided another layer of reinforcement. These included
television, radio, print,
and
online media
channels. Community radio carried discussions, testimonials, stories, and public service announcements related to swachhata.
Social media platforms
such as Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, and Instagram proved instrumental in disseminating key messages and building virtual networks and communities.
Mobile telephone services
supported awareness through bulk SMS, WhatsApp, and podcasts.
Image
6
: A social media post regarding SHS 2026 campaign
Swachh Talks
provides an example of digital engagement within SBM-U. It is a
peer-learning webinar series
for sharing field experiences and best practices related to Swachhata. Such platforms extend the conversation beyond conventional sanitation to issues like plastic waste management and promotion of the circular economy.
The movement from IPC to community mobilisation represents a shift in the
unit of behaviour change
. This progression is important to the SBCC approach under SBM. Communication does not end when a message reaches an individual. It gains greater significance when people discuss it, adapt it to their local context, and participate in collective action. In this process,
participation itself becomes a form of communication
.
Celebrity Endorsements and Popular Culture as Vehicles for SBCC
Image
7
: Celebrity Endorsements to promote toilet usage
Swachh Bharat also used the reach of celebrities to strengthen its SBCC efforts. In 2016,
Amitabh Bachchan
and
Sachin Tendulkar
featured in national audio-visual campaigns for SBM-G. These campaigns were designed to make communication more people-centric and support behaviour change and citizen engagement. Both of them also
participated in
Swachh Bharat events
to encourage grassroots workers and sanitation champions.
Amitabh Bachchan
subsequently led the
‘Darwaza Band’ campaign
in 2017. The campaign
promoted toilet use
among people who had toilets but continued to practise open defecation. It also featured
Anushka Sharma
, who
encouraged women to take leadership
in addressing sanitation within their villages. The campaign used mass media to complement grassroots IEC and interpersonal communication by Swachhagrahis.
Cinema also became a vehicle for addressing sanitation-related social norms.
‘Toilet – Ek Prem Katha’,
featuring
Akshay Kumar
and
Bhumi Pednekar
, brought sanitation and toilet use into mainstream popular culture. In 2018,
Akshay Kumar
and
Bhumi Pednekar
featured in an SBM-G campaign promoting
twin-pit toilet technology
. The film was also made available for
non-commercial screenings in villages
by state and district SBM-G teams. The campaign further used celebrity influence to address the stigma around emptying toilet pits and encourage sustained toilet use.
Vidya Balan
featured in a video propagating the slogan
“jaha soch, vaha shauchalaya”.
It stressed upon the health benefits of using toilets. It also encouraged women-led toilet-building initiatives in rural households.
Thus, popular media served as an additional layer of SBCC, taking sanitation messages from government campaigns into television, cinema and public discourse.
Women and Children: Shaping and Experiencing Swachhata
Sanitation can transform everyday experiences while creating new spaces for participation. For women,
Suraksha, Suvidha and Swabhimaan
capture three important dimensions of this change. Safety, convenience, and self-respect connect sanitation with women’s everyday lives. The impact is reflected in women’s reported experiences. A study conducted in collaboration with the Ministry of Jal Shakti found that
93 percent of women no longer feared being hurt by someone or harmed by animals while defecating
. 91 percent reported
saving up to an hour
and avoiding travel of up to a kilometre. 93 percent also reported
no longer restricting food or water intake
to manage sanitation needs.
Interestingly, in
Bihar
, people have started calling toilets ‘
Izzatghars’
, signifying their connection with the dignity of women. Construction of toilets has, thus, helped address a significant social imbalance. It is becoming a reason for economic and social empowerment. Women have contributed to sanitation as
community actors
. Women’s groups and SHGs form part of the community networks through which sanitation communication can take place. This
connects sanitation communication with existing community institutions
and networks.
Image 8
: Schools educating children about Swachhata
Children provide another important link between sanitation communication and everyday behaviour.
Schools can become spaces where sanitation practices are discussed, demonstrated and reinforced. The SBM identifies students as participants and
agents of change
. SBM has focused on
school-based approaches
including curriculum integration, awareness campaigns, Shramdaan, mobile-van education and visits to waste-management facilities. Communication has also reached children through formats that combine learning with participation and entertainment. These include
educational videos, flipcharts
and other materials for small-group engagement. It also recognises local and traditional formats such as puppet shows, magic shows, drama and street theatre for communicating sanitation messages.
Together, women and children illustrate the two-way nature of sanitation behaviour change.
They experience the benefits of improved Swachhata while also contributing to its spread through families, schools and communities.
Women’s groups may strengthen community networks, while children may carry sanitation messages into households and everyday interactions. Swachhata therefore becomes not only a matter of infrastructure or individual practice, but a shared community behaviour sustained across generations.
Reinforcing Desired Swachhata Behaviour through Awards & Recognitions
Sustaining Swachhata requires reinforcement beyond initial awareness and mobilisation. The SBM approach combines certification, recognition, nudges, and community incentives. These mechanisms help sustain participation and encourage continued adoption of desired sanitation practices.
Certification protocols
awarded to cities and villages provide measurable standards for sanitation and cleanliness outcomes. Under SBM,
ODF, ODF+, ODF++, Water+, and Star Rating protocols
helped standardise these outcomes with citizen participation. The
ODF protocol
focuses on ensuring access to toilets for all citizens.
ODF+
extends this focus to functional and usable Community and Public Toilets. Their proper operation and maintenance support continued toilet use and help prevent slippage to open defecation.
ODF++
addresses the safe containment, evacuation, transportation, and processing of faecal sludge. It seeks to prevent untreated sludge from entering open drains, water bodies or fields.
Water+
extends the focus to untreated black and grey water. It also promotes reuse of a portion of treated wastewater. For solid waste management, the
Star Rating Protocol for Garbage Free Cities
provides a single metric for assessing a city’s waste management status. Its parameters include door-to-door collection and source segregation. They also cover scientific processing of waste and remediation of legacy dumpsites. Together, these protocols create benchmarks against which Swachhata outcomes can be assessed.
Recognition
can reinforce participation by making positive behaviour visible within the community. SBM rewards and felicitates
best-performing workers, peer leaders and local champions
through
peer recognition
and
appreciation letters
from the government. Recognition can also create aspirational examples for others to emulate. The approach therefore connects individual contribution with collective identity and community participation.
Image
9
: A winner of "Give Polythene Get Gold" campaign
Incentives
can also be designed around specific local sanitation and waste management challenges. The
Swachhata Chronicles
documents an example from Panchayat Halqa Hiller in Jammu and Kashmir. The initiative introduced
“Give Polythene Get Gold”
to encourage communities to collect plastic waste. Youth and women supported the campaign, which aimed to make local areas free from polythene waste. Two gold coins were offered against specified quantities of collected plastic waste. The initiative combined awareness, community participation, and an incentive to encourage action. The campaign also included cloth bags for households and community shramdaan drives.
Thus, reinforcement under Swachhata operates at multiple levels. Protocols establish standards, nudges encourage desired actions, recognition celebrates sustained participation, and community incentives can stimulate local ownership. These mechanisms help shift Swachhata from a campaign-driven activity towards a sustained behavioural practice.
Behaviour Monitoring for Maintaining Swachhata
Sustaining Swachhata requires mechanisms that can assess progress and identify areas needing further action. Monitoring, therefore, extends beyond measuring infrastructure. It also creates opportunities for citizen participation, local assessment, and continuous improvement.
Swachh Survekshan
has emerged as the
world’s largest urban sanitation survey
. It
evaluates cities and states across sanitation and cleanliness
parameters. The survey has also evolved into an important governance tool under SBM-U. Swachh Survekshan acts as a catalyst by
encouraging healthy competition
among cities and States. This creates an incentive for local administrations to improve their sanitation performance. Citizen participation has also expanded significantly through the survey. Around
one lakh citizens provided feedback
during its first round in 2016. This increased to nearly
five crore citizens
during the sixth round in 2021. The survey therefore provides more than an assessment of sanitation outcomes. It creates a structured interface between citizens, local governments and sanitation systems.
At the community level, monitoring also supports the sustainability of behavioural change. SBM-G guidelines provide for continued engagement by
Nigrani Samitis, community leaders and Panchayat representatives
after ODF declaration.
The Continuing Journey of Swachhata
The journey of the
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)
reflects a progressive evolution in both sanitation practices and communication approaches. The initial emphasis was on creating awareness and generating demand for household toilets, followed by efforts to encourage their regular use and eliminate open defecation. As these gains were consolidated, the focus expanded towards sustaining
ODF status
and strengthening the management of solid and liquid waste. Communication evolved alongside these priorities, moving from awareness generation to deeper engagement and collective participation.
Collectively, these experiences reflect a consistent trajectory, from
information to engagement, from engagement to participation, and from participation to sustained community ownership
. Under SBM, communication has consequently become an integral part of the sanitation ecosystem, connecting people with infrastructure, institutions, and collective action. The larger objective is not merely to communicate the message of
Swachhata
, but to
nurture it as a sustained practice embedded in everyday community life.

title: Dignity by Design: Innovation Reshapes India's Public Toilets
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 OCT 2026 12:33PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Over the years, India’s cities have made significant strides in expanding access to public sanitation facilities. From improving availability and cleanliness to enhancing safety and accessibility, cities are adopting innovative approaches to make public toilets more inclusive and user-friendly.
Building on these efforts, the
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM)
, launched on
2 October 2014
, has advanced sanitation innovation across India. Cities built toilets, raised awareness and worked towards becoming
Open Defecation Free (ODF)
. Many went further, achieving ODF+ and ODF++ status. In 2022, the Toilets 2.0 initiative under Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U) raised the bar again. Its aim was to make Community and Public Toilets (CT/PTs) safe, clean and inviting for everyone. Citizens can now find the nearest facility through the
‘SBM Toilet Locator’
on the Swachhata app.
Today, the change is visible in unexpected places. An old bus has become a women's toilet. Plastic waste has turned into building material. A busy market now hosts a smart lounge. A small city has found a safe way to handle sanitary waste. Pilgrim towns offer facilities open to all. Together, these stories trace the journey from basic access to dignity, safety and innovation.
New Age Toilets: A Scrap Bus Becomes a Safe Space for Women
Women travelling through crowded bus terminals often struggle to find a clean and private toilet. In
Bengaluru, Karnataka
, an old bus found a new purpose to meet this need. The
Sthree Toilet
was set up at the Majestic bus terminal of the
Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC)
. Built from a scrap vehicle, it serves women exclusively.
The toilet has
three Indian-style and two Western-style commodes
. A
sanitary napkin vending machine
and an
incinerator
support menstrual hygiene. A dedicated space lets mothers feed their babies and change diapers. Sensor lights run on
solar power generated by the facility itself
. Waste drains into the nearest sewage chamber at the bus station. The toilet has proved especially helpful for mothers travelling with young children.
Navi Mumbai’s Sustainable Toilets: A Model of Eco-Conscious Urban Design
Can a public toilet be built from what a city throws away? Navi Mumbai has shown that it can. The
Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation (NMMC)
has developed
Aspirational Toilets
at Sector 14, Koparkhairane. The site lies near the Nisargudyan urban garden, a busy public space. Around
8,000 to 9,000 visitors
use the facility every day.
The structure uses
426 square metres of recycled plastic sheeting
. This includes
5.3 metric tonnes of single-use plastic
, 11,700 plastic bottles and 35,200 bottle caps. Builders also reused
85 repurposed computer keyboards
and
284 kg of scrap metal
. The project puts the principle of
Reduce, Reuse and Recycle
into everyday practice.
Safety and comfort are built into the design. Separate sections for men and women ensure privacy. Units for children and persons with disabilities, baby care stations and sanitary pad vending machines serve all users. A
fountain running on treated sewage water
completes its green design. The complex now stands as a symbol of environmental innovation and civic pride.
Swachh Smart Toilets: Freshrooms Bring Comfort to Bhopal
Shoppers, vendors and commuters crowd Bhopal’s
10 Number Market
every day. The Bhopal Municipal Corporation has set up
‘Freshrooms’, smart and luxury public convenience centres
. They follow a
Design-Build-Operate-Transfer (DBOT)
model under a
Public-Private Partnership (PPP)
. The Smart Lounge at the market covers 800 to 1,000 square feet. It serves
500 to 1,000 visitors daily
.
Technology lies at the heart of the facility. It offers
sensor-based toilets
and
touch-free urinals
. Visitors can also use hot and cold showers, lockers and Wi-Fi. A café, vending machines and baby-changing rooms add to the comfort. A
digital information wall
keeps users informed. Separate, accessible facilities serve men, women and persons with disabilities.
By integrating technology, comfort and sustainability, Freshrooms demonstrate how innovative models can deliver world-class sanitation while ensuring financial self-sufficiency
.
Smart Sanitary Solutions in Karad: Safe Disposal, Safer City
Clean toilets are one part of the sanitation story. Safe disposal of sanitary waste is another. Used napkins and diapers, if dumped openly, harm health and the environment. Stigma often keeps the issue hidden.
Karad
, a small city in Satara district of
Maharashtra
, has tackled this challenge head-on. It ensures
100% segregation, collection and processing
of sanitary and biomedical waste. Nearly
300 to 350 kg of sanitary waste
is collected daily from hospitals, clinics, households and other facilities.
The first step was to break the taboo around sanitary waste. Workshops, community outreach and public announcements explained the risks of careless disposal. The
Karad Municipal Council (KMC)
worked with women residents to form awareness groups. These groups carried the message across residential areas. Separate
red bins
were placed in public toilets to make safe disposal easier for women.
Schools were encouraged to install sanitary pad vending machines and disposal systems. The city’s
Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
team urged users to wrap used pads in paper. Many schools have since installed incinerators. Their residue goes to the biomedical waste treatment plant.
Garbage collection vehicles carry a
separate bin for sanitary waste
. Staff sort this waste so that only suitable material reaches the incinerator.
KMC has partnered with the
Karad Hospital Association
to treat this waste. KMC allocated land for construction of the biomedical waste treatment plant, while the association operates and maintains it. This is a
600 kg/day Common Biomedical Waste Treatment Facility (CBWTF)
. It processes the sanitary waste collected by the council free of charge. Its central incinerator reaches temperatures of
up to 1,200°C
. Gases are filtered to remove harmful substances. Emissions are monitored in real time and linked to the
State Pollution Control Board (SPCB)
system.
This PPP partnership has eased the council’s financial burden, as it bears only collection and transport costs. High-temperature incineration of sanitary waste has reduced health risks and protects sanitation workers handling the waste. Open dumping has been eliminated, preventing environmental contamination and reducing the spread of diseases. It has improved residents’ quality of life, particularly for women affected by sanitary waste disposal challenges.
Comfort, Cleanliness & Care for Tirupati’s Pilgrims
Places of faith draw lakhs of visitors, making clean toilets a daily necessity.
Tirupati
is among India’s busiest pilgrimage destinations. The
Tirupati Municipal Corporation
has built modern toilet complexes for devotees, tourists and residents.
A dedicated
Pink Toilet Complex
for women stands near the bus station. It links key points such as Srinivasam, Vishnuvasam, the railway station and the bus terminal. Women can use Indian and Western toilets, restrooms, and mother care and changing rooms. Incinerators and sanitary napkin vending machines support menstrual hygiene. The complex serves
12,000 to 15,000 users daily
. A structured three-shift cleaning system maintains the facility.
A Common Public Toilet Complex near the railway station caters to
20,000–25,000 devotees
visiting the Govindarajaswamy Temple area daily. Designed for universal access, it provides
dedicated facilities
for men, women, transgender persons, Divyaang, and children. Ramps, handrails, child-friendly fixtures, and bathing rooms ensure
greater comfort, hygiene, and accessibility for pilgrims
.
Road Ahead
Under SBM-U 2.0, the focus has moved beyond building toilets. The goal now is to keep them clean, safe, inclusive and sustainable. These stories show how cities are reaching that goal in their own ways. A scrap bus, recycled plastic, sensor-based fixtures and a high-temperature incinerator each play a part. Partnerships with private operators, hospitals and communities keep these facilities running well. Dedicated workers and caretakers give them life every day. As the
Swachh Bharat Mission
completes twelve years, the direction is clear. Every citizen, whatever their gender, ability or location, deserves a clean and dignified toilet. From markets to monuments, Indian cities are turning that promise into reality.

title: Urban Transformation: Building Greener, More Sustainable Cities
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 OCT 2026 11:57AM by PIB Delhi
content:
A city’s growth is visible not only in its buildings and roads, but also in how it responds to everyday challenges. The way waste is handled, communities participate and services are delivered can shape the quality of urban life. The
Swachh Bharat Mission
has given this everyday transformation a strong foundation across the country. Over time, the focus has moved beyond simply collecting and disposing of waste. Cities are finding ways to recover value from discarded material, encourage responsible habits and make municipal services more efficient. Green practices are also gaining ground as segregation, recycling, reuse and recovery become integral to local systems. Digital monitoring, data-driven systems and better service delivery are helping local bodies to work with greater precision. These efforts are gradually creating urban spaces that balance environmental responsibility with the needs of everyday life.
Cities Leading the Way in Sustainable Urban Transformation
Across different regions, cities are demonstrating how local solutions can translate into meaningful environmental outcomes. Their experiences show that sustainable urban transformation can take many forms. These include converting dumping grounds into integrated waste management facilities and promoting zero-waste practices. Technology is also improving everyday sanitation services and strengthening urban systems. The following stories highlight these diverse approaches.
A Greener Goa: Turning Waste into Energy
Located in the valleys of Saligao, Goa, the Integrated Waste Management Facility Center promotes environmental sustainability. Spread across
113,000 square metres
, it is operated by the Goa Waste Management Corporation (GWMC). The facility was formerly used as a garbage dump. It has now been transformed into an integrated, eco-friendly waste management hub for Goa. The center manages
250 metric tons
of wet and dry waste every day. At this plant, organic matter is separated from waste and converted into biogas, which helps
generate electricity
. This energy supports the needs of the local community by alleviating power shortages in the area.
Wet waste from restaurants is converted into valuable bioproducts, including methane-rich biogas. Recyclable materials are recovered from
100 metric tons
of dry waste processed at the facility. The remaining dry waste is sent to cement factories for co-processing. Additionally, 1.32 kilowatts of electricity is generated from wet waste at the facility. This electricity powers 35 units, with half supplied to the Goa Electricity Department. The plant also generates 7–8 tons of compost daily. Local panchayats use this compost for gardening and reforestation projects.
The integrated solid waste management facility is strengthening Goa’s waste management system, processing approximately
one-third of the state's total waste
. People who once merely collected waste are now part of the plant's trained workforce. This provides livelihood opportunities for several families in the region while benefiting the environment.
The plant operates continuously throughout the year, aiming to make the city "zero waste”.
Gandhinagar’s Zero-Waste Journey: Citizens Driving Change
Gandhinagar in Gujarat stands as a strong example of swachhata and sustainability. Through its commitment to the Swachh Bharat Mission and participation in Swachh Survekshan, the city promotes a culture of cleanliness. Inspired by the global
Zero Waste Week
movement, the Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation organised impactful activities from 2nd to 7th September, 2026. These initiatives aimed to encourage behavioural change and promote the 3R principles:
Reduce, Reuse and Recycle
. Activities were conducted at 25 locations across the city, directly engaging more than 600 citizens. Targeted social media campaigns further reached and sensitised over
40,000 individuals
during the week. The My Theli stalls became vibrant spaces for community participation and sustainable action across Gandhinagar. Citizens were encouraged to donate used clothes. Skilled women from local self-help groups transformed these donations into reusable carry bags.
The “
Swachhata Se Shuruvat
” campaign was launched to encourage responsible practices among school students. Quiz competitions were organised to raise awareness about environmental concerns and responsible practices. Engaging and interactive games were designed through which students gained practical insights into sustainability. The Reduce, Reuse, Recycle van visited residents at their doorsteps to collect old clothes, plastic and electronic waste. Participants received rewards for their donations, encouraging greater community involvement. Citizens were also invited to share their personal efforts and daily practices through online testimonials. Through these initiatives, Gandhinagar is advancing its zero-waste vision. The city continues to strengthen resource-conscious practices while working towards the goal of Garbage Free Cities.
Kakinada’s Smart Approach to Efficient Waste Management
In Andhra Pradesh’s East Godavari District, Kakinada has emerged as a notable example of technology-enabled waste management. Kakinada generates around
144 tons
of waste daily, comprising wet, dry and hazardous materials. The Kakinada Municipal Corporation manages this operation across 50 wards, which are further divided into 382 micro pockets. Each micro pocket covers 250 to 350 households and is managed by two sanitation workers.
With around
112,993 households
, over 973 sanitation workers have been employed to manage waste. These households are strategically organised into
40,661
designated waste collection points across the city. Digital tools are used to streamline waste collection and transportation. The Online Waste Management System (OWMS) tracks the process in real time. Radio Frequency Identification (RFID), facial recognition, GPS and a human resource management system (HRMS) further support workforce and transportation management.
RFID chip-enabled tags
are installed at the gates of every waste generator. Collectors scan these tags when waste is picked up. The scanned information is recorded in the OWMS, enabling officials to monitor collection progress. Continuous monitoring and dedicated sanitation staff have helped the system achieve
100% door-to-door collection
.
The Municipal Corporation has deployed 108 hopper vehicles equipped with GPS tracking devices. These monitor the transportation and report deviations during waste collection and transportation to processing plants. It has also introduced a
Facial Recognition System (FRS)
for all SafaiMitras. Workers can now record their attendance using facial recognition technology. This eliminates the need for manual attendance registers or fingerprint scanners. All these technologies are integrated into a Central Command Centre for close monitoring. Around
60%
of residents now segregate waste at source. The combined efforts of sanitation workers and residents are strengthening Kakinada’s ability to manage its waste efficiently.
Ghaziabad: Turning Waste into Carbon Value
Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, is advancing cleanliness and urban development while taking steps to reduce carbon emissions. The Ghaziabad Municipal Corporation (GMC) has registered for an international carbon credit project. The initiative is verified by the United Nations and combines environmental protection with potential financial benefits. Improved solid waste management under the Swachh Bharat Mission can
reduce greenhouse gases
such as methane from dumping sites.
Greater use of clean fuels and energy sources can also lower dependence on fossil fuels and reduce carbon emissions. In line with these efforts, the Ghaziabad Municipal Corporation has demonstrated its commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals. It has been accredited under the
Verified Carbon Standard (VCS)
, supported by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
The GMC has replaced old streetlights across the city with energy-efficient LED lights. This measure reduces carbon emissions while also lowering electricity consumption. It is also adopting "wet waste composting" to produce compost from wet waste. This process supports faster waste management and helps reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Following Indore in Madhya Pradesh, Ghaziabad is set to become the first urban local body (ULB) in Uttar Pradesh and the second in the country to turn waste into a new source of value.
Together, these measures are expected to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by approximately
2.7 lakh tonnes
. This reduction corresponds to
2.7 lakh carbon credits
, with one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent to one credit. Certified credits can be converted into revenue by being sold on the international carbon market. The initiative supports cleanliness, environmental protection and economic opportunities for Ghaziabad.
Building Cities That Value Every Resource
The transformation underway across cities reflects a broader shift in the way urban resources are managed. Technology is strengthening everyday sanitation services while citizens are becoming active participants in sustainable practices. Local solutions are creating visible improvements in everyday urban life. They also show the value of combining innovation with people’s efforts for effective waste management. Together, these approaches point towards urban systems that are not only cleaner, but also more circular and resource-efficient

content:
In pursuance of the guidelines issued by the Government, the Department of Pharmaceuticals (DoP), along with its attached and subordinate organizations - including the
National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), Pharmaceuticals & Medical Devices Bureau of India (PMBI), National Institutes of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPERs), and Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)
- officially commenced
Special Campaign 6,
on the occasion of
Gandhi Jayanti, on October 2, 2026
.
Following an intensive
Preparatory Phase (September 15–30, 2026)
where baseline targets, site identifications, and record inventories were successfully completed, the Department has now transitioned into the
active implementation phase
running upto
October 31, 2026
.
Campaign Metrics & Baseline Targets for Special Campaign 6:
Cleanliness Campaigns: 12,208
cleanliness and outstation office drives scheduled across organizational units.
Pendency & Grievance Redressal Targets:
Active resolution tracking is underway for 4 MP references, 2 Parliamentary Assurances, 1 Inter-Ministerial Cabinet proposal, 58 State Government references, 2 PMO references, 72 Public Grievances (CPGRAMS), 18 Public Grievance Appeals, and 20 Easing of Rules/Process items.
Record Management:
Review of 2,716 physical files and 20 e-files to optimize workspace and streamline documentation.
Scientific E-Waste Management:
Systematic disposal targeting an aggregate of
1,011 quantities
of obsolete equipment - including 602 units of IT & telecommunication equipment, 196 consumer electrical/electronic & photovoltaic units, 53 large/small electrical appliances, 5 laboratory instruments, 154 other electronic assets, and electrical tools, through MoEFCC - empanelled recyclers.
Key Focus Areas:
Scientific E-Waste Management:
Safe segregation and disposal, compliant with E-Waste Management Rules.
Pendency Liquidation:
Swift closure of public grievances, parliamentary assurances, and official references.
Space Optimization:
Promoting clean, clutter-free working environments through systematic record reviews and scrap clearance.
The Department remains committed to institutionalizing
Swachhata
and elevating governance standards throughout this month-long nationwide initiative. Daily progress updates and best practices will be shared via the national SCDPM portal.
